title: One Square Meter
clue: A patch of ground no bigger than a bath mat holds more news than a whole street, and one of you reads it faster.
reveal: Pick one small patch of ground and give it a whole visit. Your dog reads it nose-first at their own pace while you read it your way, eyes and fingertips. Then you compare notes and take one photo of the square from above.
objective: Let your dog choose one square meter near home, give it an unhurried visit, compare what you each found and take one photo from above.
instructions: The evening before: put a marker by the door. A scarf, a dish towel or a bath mat will do. It is for you only, never a boundary for your dog. Pocket three prompts for your own turn: something tiny, something moving, something that was here before today.

Set out on a loose leash for a short wander near home, with no destination. Let your dog choose the square: the first patch where they slow down and read properly, not just a quick sniff. Pick grass, verge or clean sidewalk away from roads, and skip anywhere with litter, glass, spilled food or dog mess. Nothing grabbing them? Your own doorstep or a spot beside a bench is a fine square.
Lay your marker round the spot, about an arm-span each way. Your dog can step in, out or round it, and nobody is asked to stay put. Keep the leash loose and your voice quiet.

Dog's turn. Stand or sit still and say nothing. Watch where the nose spends longest: a corner, a crack, one tuft. Stay until your dog moves on. That may be two minutes or fifteen, and a quick finish is a real answer.

Your turn. Lower yourself beside the square, or lean over it from a bench, and look for your three prompts. Touch nothing that is alive and take nothing home. If your dog starts to eat something, calmly move on; no square is worth a mystery snack.

Compare. Was there a spot your dog read for ages where you could see nothing at all? That is the square's secret. Take your photo from above, standing, with the marker's edge in frame. If the square is hard texture (paving, a drain cover, brick), you can also lay a sheet over it once your dog has moved on and make a crayon rubbing for a Square Book: a folder or envelope that is never full.

Close the square: pick up the marker and shake it out, so the ground goes back to being ordinary sidewalk. Take one step back, look once, then head home whichever way your dog fancies, for water and a proper rest.
twist: You read the same patch twice, once the dog's way and once yours, and the spot where the two readings disagree becomes the photo.
variations: Seated version: choose a square within reach of a bench or your doorstep chair. Stay seated for both turns, and use your phone's zoom for your own look.

No outdoors today? Lay a dish towel on the floor with a few dry leaves and twigs from a safe place outside (no berries, mushrooms or unknown plants). Your dog reads it while you watch, and you take it away if they start chewing.
For a senior or slow-moving dog: choose a square just outside your gate, keep the whole visit under ten minutes and add a rest on a blanket afterwards.
For a dog who keeps moving: let the walk carry on and read the square yourself while they roam the verge on a long, loose leash.
completion: Your dog has finished with the square in their own time, even if that was quick, and you have taken the overhead photo and shaken out the marker.
photoIdea: From above and a step back with the marker's edge in frame, catching whatever your dog was reading if they allow it. A nose or paw in the corner is a bonus.
memoryPrompt: What was in that square that you would have walked straight past?
supplies: A scarf, dish towel or bath mat as a marker
A leash and harness or collar your dog already wears
optionalSupplies: Small bag for any litter you find
Paper and a crayon for a rubbing
substitutes: No scarf? A folded bath mat or dish towel makes a good square.
No magnifier? Your phone camera zoomed in works as one.
safety: Hand-test the sidewalk before you stop (too hot for you is too hot for paws) and skip frosty or salted ground.
Keep your dog from eating food scraps, plants or litter, and keep crayons out of reach; use a leash.
If a stranger or another dog comes near, calmly leave and politely decline petting or feeding.
